paragraphs.title: Joy in Going Up to Jerusalem and the City’s Formation

answers: Being told to go into the house of the LORD
Sitting in a royal palace
Winning a battle
easy.explanation: The psalmist says, “I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the LORD.”

answers: To the gates of the city
Into the house of the LORD
To the house of David
easy.explanation: The invitation was to go into the house of the LORD.
easy.q: Where were they planning to go?

answers: As an empty city
As a divided city
As a city joined together
easy.explanation: Jerusalem is described as “a city that is compact together.”

answers: Hearing the invitation, arriving at the gates, and seeing Jerusalem as a united city
Seeing the city, leaving it, and then receiving an invitation
Building the city, leaving its gates, and becoming sorrowful
medium.explanation: The psalm begins with joy at the invitation, then describes standing at Jerusalem’s gates and seeing the city joined together.
medium.q: What order of events is described in these verses?

answers: That the city was built in the wilderness
That the parts of the city appeared joined into one
That the city had no gates
medium.explanation: The phrase emphasizes the unity and close joining of the city.
medium.q: What does the phrase “a city that is compact together” suggest?

answers: Their feet stand within its gates
They sit on the thrones of judgment
They leave the city immediately
medium.explanation: The psalm says, “Our feet shall stand within thy gates, O Jerusalem.”
medium.q: What happens when the travelers reach Jerusalem?

answers: The joyful invitation leads to an actual arrival in Jerusalem
The joy comes from leaving Jerusalem
The two verses have no connection
challenge.explanation: The invitation to go to the LORD’s house is followed by the travelers actually standing within Jerusalem’s gates.
challenge.q: What connection exists between the joy in verse 1 and the arrival in verse 2?

answers: The city was built without inhabitants
David may have joined separate areas into one city
The tribes divided the city into new sections
challenge.explanation: The idea describes Jerusalem as appearing united, possibly because David joined previously separate areas.
challenge.q: What might explain the description of Jerusalem as a city joined together?

answers: The movement from intention to actual arrival
The movement from joy to sorrow
The movement from Jerusalem to another city
challenge.explanation: The verses move from the desire or invitation to go to the experience of standing at Jerusalem’s gates.
challenge.q: What does the movement from “Let us go” to “Our feet shall stand” emphasize?

paragraphs.title: Jerusalem as the Center of All Israel and the City of Judgment and Kingship

answers: The tribes
David alone
Only the people who live in the city
easy.explanation: The psalm says, “Whither the tribes go up, the tribes of the LORD.”

answers: To build a wall
To give thanks unto the name of the LORD
To leave Jerusalem
easy.explanation: The tribes go up “to give thanks unto the name of the LORD.”
easy.q: Why do the tribes go up?

answers: Only gates
Only private homes
Thrones of judgment and thrones of the house of David
easy.explanation: Verse 5 mentions “thrones of judgment” and “the thrones of the house of David.”
easy.q: What is found in Jerusalem according to verse 5?

answers: It is a center for all Israel
Only one tribe is important there
It is a place from which the people depart
medium.explanation: The tribes of the LORD gather there, showing Jerusalem’s importance to all Israel.
medium.q: What does the gathering of the tribes suggest about Jerusalem?

answers: A marketplace and a residential area
A sacred center and a place of judgment and kingship
A battlefield and a place of exile
medium.explanation: The tribes give thanks there, and the city contains the thrones of judgment and the house of David.
medium.q: What combination of roles does Jerusalem have in these verses?

answers: To fulfill a testimony or ordinance for Israel and give thanks to the LORD
To count the city’s gates
To appoint new royal thrones
medium.explanation: The tribes go up “unto the testimony of Israel, to give thanks unto the name of the LORD.”
medium.q: What is the purpose of the tribes’ gathering in Jerusalem?

answers: The tribes go there, and it contains the seats of judgment and royal authority
The verses describe only its fields
The verses present it as an isolated town
challenge.explanation: All the tribes are connected with Jerusalem, and the city contains the thrones of judgment and the house of David.
challenge.q: How do verses 4–5 present Jerusalem as a national center?

answers: Together they show Jerusalem’s spiritual and public importance
They describe two places unrelated to Jerusalem
Giving thanks removes the need for kingship
challenge.explanation: The verses connect worship, judgment, and royal authority in the same central city.
challenge.q: What relationship exists between giving thanks to the LORD and the thrones of judgment?

answers: Its thrones are set in Jerusalem
It goes up with every tribe
It builds the gates of the city
challenge.explanation: The verse specifically says, “the thrones of the house of David.”
challenge.q: What detail about the house of David is specifically mentioned?

paragraphs.title: A Prayer for the Peace of Jerusalem

answers: Pray for the peace of Jerusalem
Build a new city
Leave Jerusalem
easy.explanation: The psalm says, “Pray for the peace of Jerusalem.”
easy.q: What does the psalmist ask people to do?

answers: Those who leave the city
Those who love Jerusalem
Only the house of David
easy.explanation: The verse says, “they shall prosper that love thee,” speaking of Jerusalem.
easy.q: Who will prosper according to verse 6?

answers: For his brethren and companions
For foreign kings
For the gatekeepers only
easy.explanation: He says, “For my brethren and companions’ sakes, I will now say, Peace be within thee.”
easy.q: For whose sake does the psalmist speak peace?

answers: War and rivalry
Peace and prosperity
Abandonment and desolation
medium.explanation: He prays, “Peace be within thy walls, and prosperity within thy palaces.”
medium.q: What does the psalmist desire within Jerusalem’s walls and palaces?

answers: The city’s boundaries and defenses
The tribes of Israel
The royal thrones
medium.explanation: The word “walls” refers to the city’s protective boundaries and defenses.
medium.q: In verse 7, what does “walls” most directly refer to?

answers: Because of the house of the LORD his God
For the sake of the city’s trade
So that the tribes will leave
medium.explanation: He says, “Because of the house of the LORD our God I will seek thy good.”
medium.q: Why will the psalmist seek Jerusalem’s good?

answers: From Jerusalem to those who love her, to the psalmist’s brethren and companions, and to the house of the LORD
From the house of the LORD to another city only
From the tribes to abandoning Jerusalem
challenge.explanation: The prayer includes Jerusalem, her lovers, the psalmist’s companions, and the house of the LORD.
challenge.q: How does the circle of concern expand in verses 6–9?

answers: He seeks the good of others and of the sacred city
He wants peace only for himself
He opposes the welfare of Jerusalem
challenge.explanation: His prayer is motivated by concern for Jerusalem, its people, his companions, and the house of the LORD.
challenge.q: What does the repeated concern for peace reveal about the psalmist’s motives?

answers: The city’s peace includes security and prosperity for those who live in and love it
Peace concerns only the city’s buildings
The city has no connection with those who love it
challenge.explanation: The psalm joins peace within the city to prosperity for those who love Jerusalem.
challenge.q: What relationship is shown between Jerusalem’s peace and the welfare of its people?
